title: Giulio Ciccone Questions European Championships Photo Finish Against Remco Evenepoel
author: ahood
text:
Ciccone reacts after losing the European Championships in a photo finish. (Photo: Getty Images)

Giulio Ciccone wants to see the image that decided the European road title for himself, because he still has doubts about Sunday’s razor-thin defeat .

The Italian said he still cannot come to terms with the photo finish verdict and footage of his dramatic loss against Remco Evenepoel .

“The title was awarded by a margin of 0.0028 seconds, or 2.8 thousandths of a second,” Ciccone wrote on Instagram.

“I’ve watched the available footage hundreds of times and, in the shots where the finish line is visible, I keep seeing something that I cannot reconcile with that verdict.”

Evenepoel snagged gold Sunday with a spectacular bike throw in Slovenia to edge out the Italian in a two-up sprint so tight that it took a photo finish to call the winner.

On Monday, Ciccone praised the Belgian’s performance and defended his racing tactics, but said he wanted to see the evidence for himself.

“Remco was the strongest rider yesterday,” he wrote. “I’m asking for something very simple: to see the photo finish at the actual finish line.”

Ciccone said commissaires and federation technical staff explained Monday morning how the photo finish works and the criteria used to interpret it.

But that’s not enough for the 31-year-old Lidl-Trek star to accept the outcome.

“So I’m not asking for another explanation,” he wrote. “I’m asking to see the photo finish that corresponds exactly to the actual finish line.”

Ciccone’s questions followed a brutally close finish to Sunday’s wild and wide-open European Championship.

Ciccone and Evenepoel dueled to the end, with the Italian looking to have the winning edge after out-positioning the Belgian on the final corner. Evenepoel opened up a desperate burst in the closing meters and timed his bike throw perfectly at the line.

After a long and tense wait, the race jury eventually awarded the victory to Evenepoel.

In a lengthy public post on Monday, the Italian said he wants to see the photo of both wheels crossing the line.

“Because if a European title is decided by 2.8 thousandths of a second, I believe it is legitimate to ask for that crossing to be shown with the same precision used to determine the result,” he wrote.

“If that image confirms the verdict, there will be nothing more to add,” he wrote. “But until I’m shown that correspondence, a question remains for me that has yet to be answered.”

On Monday evening, the Union Européenne de Cyclisme — which runs and organizes the European championships — issued the following statement:

“The Union Européenne de Cyclisme (UEC) informs that the photo-finish system used at the 2026 UEC Road European Championships (EtherLynx Vision PRO X) records the finish line thousands of times per second (13,000 in the specific case of the European Championship races), making it possible to determine the finishing order with extreme precision, even when the differences are minimal,” a media note read.

“It is important to clarify that a photo finish is not a traditional photograph. The final image is composed of the chronological sequence of recordings made at the finish line; for this reason, the horizontal axis represents time, not distance. This can create apparent distortions of wheels, bicycles and riders, without any impact on the accuracy of the result.

“In cycling, the determining reference is the most advanced part (tangent) of the front wheel at the moment it reaches the finish line. At the European Championships, two independent photo-finish systems were used, providing two separate images to verify the result.”

title: Gabriel in Man Utd team photo but no hint of reconciliation
text:
JJ Gabriel has been included in Manchester United's official team photo for this season but there remains no hint of a reconciliation with the club as new details of his efforts to leave Old Trafford emerge.

The teenage forward - who turns 16 on Tuesday - features in the photographs that were released on Monday.

It is understood the pictures were taken on 8 September - two days before he played his final game for the club and informed them of his intention to leave.

It is virtually certain his next involvement in a United game will be as an opposition player.

United still hold his registration and, according to sources close to Old Trafford, the club have made multiple attempts to reconcile the situation as part of their duty of care to the teenager. So far, it has been to no avail.

Gabriel is now a target for several of Europe's top clubs, with Real Madrid and Barcelona among those taking a keen interest. He now has a European Union passport, which is thought could smooth his passage to the continent.

However, while no clubs have approached United so far, they would consider legal action if any evidence of an illegal inducement by a club or agent - that would contravene regulations in relation to young players - was to emerge.

While tensions between Gabriel's camp and United had been simmering for a number of months, sources have told BBC Sport the player's decision to seek a move away was ultimately triggered by his non-inclusion in Michael Carrick’s side for the Champions League encounter with Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK on 10 September.

The youngster's camp had expressed a desire for Gabriel to be used as a substitute against Sabah - which, on paper, was the easiest of United's league-phase games.

Sources say the prospect of the Londoner coming on against Brighton in the EFL Cup on 16 September was also discussed, with United officials subsequently insistent that was the plan.

Had he played in either match, Gabriel would have become United's youngest ever player.

However, by the time the encounter with Fabian Hurzeler's side arrived, the striker had already told the club of his intention to quit and had left the country.

Gabriel could not play against Sabah because he had not been registered on United's Uefa A list of players when it was announced on 3 September. The precise reasons for this have not been made clear.

It did not prevent him scoring a hat-trick in a Uefa Youth League game against them at Leigh Sports Village earlier on 10 September. While he has not been back to United since, it is not clear whether anything significant happened after that game.

For their part, United believe they made it clear they view Gabriel as immensely important to their first-team future, even though sources have indicated the player did not report for the start of the academy's pre-season training schedule at the beginning of July - a week earlier than the senior squad - despite being asked to do so.

Sources also say they lobbied the Premier League to allow the forward to use "JJ Gabriel" on the back of his shirt - which they believe underlined their commitment to the academy prospect.

Gabriel's real name is Joseph Junior Andreou O'Cearuill - but he is reported to have changed his name for commercial purposes.

In addition, United say they have provided Gabriel with first-team care and services - included regular meetings with senior coaches and nutritionists.

That he was included in the senior team photo is also viewed as further evidence of their commitment to his development and transition into first-team football.

When Gabriel committed himself to United in the summer of 2025, the lure of breaking through at United, and the targets he could aim for, was strong.

He was only 14 at the time but already he was looking towards the first team. Within a couple of months, Gabriel was called into senior training sessions by Ruben Amorim.

Expectation grew to such an extent that interim boss Darren Fletcher was asked if it was possible the forward could make his competitive bow in the FA Cup third-round tie with Brighton in January.

Fletcher - then Gabriel's coach at under-18 level - said no, believing the youngster wasn't physically ready.

However, as he continued to excel at under-18 level, it seemed a case of when, not if, Gabriel would be given his chance.

He ended the 2025-26 campaign as the Premier League's Under-18 player of the year and picked up the same award at United. It seemed certain he would be involved at the start of pre-season, when the majority of United's senior players would be absent after their World Cup exertions.

What happened instead solidified existing doubts of those close to Gabriel that United were the right club for him.

First, he was not part of Carrick's squad for the trip to Helsinki to face Wrexham in a friendly. On 24 July, he was an unused substitute against Rosenborg in Trondheim, a match in which Carrick made 10 outfield changes. Five of those players have since been sold or loaned out.

Gabriel finally got his chance against Atletico Madrid in Stockholm on 1 August, when he replaced Bryan Mbeumo for the final eight minutes.

That turned out to be it. He was on the bench for the final two games against Leeds and AC Milan, but did not get on. Against Leeds, former FA Youth Cup team-mate Dan Armer and 18-year-old newcomer Tynan Thompson were both introduced.

Doubts over Gabriel's physicality persisted, but his performances at under-21 level made a compelling argument he was ready.

Brighton was mentioned as a potential senior debut, but the perils around that made, for those close to Gabriel, the Champions League encounter with Sabah a better option.

The theory was correct. United beat them 4-0 and Carrick had used all five substitutes by the 72nd minute. The following week, United threw away a 2-0 lead and lost against Brighton.…

title: Silca Protocol RCR 29 Review: Go Bigger
author: Josh Ross
text:
Comfortable ride feel Excellent dry cornering grip High puncture resistance for a race tire Competitive weight-to-width ratio Aerodynamically optimized width Excellent choice in 38mm size

Silca recently launched a new series of tires. The lineup covers both road and gravel, and everything offered is focused on high volume and ride feel. Of course, they launched without much of a bang, and there definitely weren’t any major claims made… No, I am obviously kidding. This is Silca, and these tires launched to so much hype it hurt. The claim was that they were head and shoulders above the rest of the field.

Then Bicycle Rolling Resistance put the RCR 29 through its testing regime, and the results were… a bit lackluster. Big claims have now been made on the other side of the fence, but not that many people have actually ridden these tires. I’ve now got a few hundred miles on them, and I think there’s more to these tires than a drum test—but I don’t love everything. Let’s look at the good and the bad when it comes to the Silca RCR 29 road tires.

What I do on a bike—almost always a race bike—is ride it longer than anyone expects. I want a tire that soaks up rough pavement, but I’m not running 34mm tires because I also want aerodynamics in a straight line, and I’m not interested in increasing wheel width (meaning weight) to optimize for a wider tire. In other words, I want to have my cake and eat it too.

I’ve been running the Silca 29mm tires at 52 psi on a 22.5mm internal width rim, and to me, they pull this balance off. A 29mm width matches well with modern rims in terms of the Rule of 105 and aerodynamics. That 29mm also means if you are a stickler for following ETRTO recommendations, you can run a 25mm internal width rim, but that’s not something I worry about.

Where I find the Silca tires really shining is cornering in the dry. Bicycle Rolling Resistance doesn’t test dry cornering because it’s universally quite high, but these tires have tested high in wet grip. Personally, I don’t care a ton about wet grip because these are on a bike that won’t see much rain, but I do think there’s nuance in dry pavement cornering grip, and these land in my “good bucket.”

Lean the bike, stand on the outside pedal, and you can feel the bite. Over and over, I surprised myself by cutting tight switchbacks a little tighter than I normally would, while still feeling confident and in control. A big part of this feeling goes back to a tire that does a great job soaking up bumps. Even on a stiff race bike, I don’t find the front wheel coming off the line over small cracks.

That means the real advantage again goes back to that ride feel, but sometimes that is accompanied by the puncture protection of an overinflated water balloon. That’s not the case here. Even before the BRR testing, I had a guess that it was decent based on the 2.1mm tread thickness. That matches the GP5000 thickness, and while thickness isn’t an exact 1:1 for puncture protection, it’s a decent way of setting expectations. BRR confirmed exactly what I expected, although it is a bit lower than the P Zero Race RS (which is also thicker). My own experience here is that all of the popular race tires are pretty close in puncture protection, and it’s good enough. Silca falls in line.

Basically, the Silca tire falls into the “good enough” bucket. I told you it has good ride feel, cornering grip, and puncture protection, and that should be enough, right? It is enough, but why are you choosing the Silca tire?

The Continental GP5000, Schwalbe Pro One, Pirelli P Zero Race RS, Goodyear Eagle F1 R Z29 Aero, and Vittoria Corsa Pro are all good tires with slight advantages and disadvantages. Maybe one leans a little this way and another a little that way, but it’s incredibly close. I doubt I can convince dedicated Vittoria fans to switch to the Zipp/Goodyear tire, and equally, for what reason would you switch from your favorite tire to the Silca? What is the unique selling proposition for Silca?

Given that Silca is all about marginal gains, I really wanted to see these come out as an aero-optimized tire. I’ve talked to Josh Poertner about aero tires plenty this year, and I know he believes in them, but the RCR is not an aero tire. When I asked for clarification, the answer was that, at this point, he doesn’t have a way to add aero gains without losing rolling resistance.

It’s a fair answer and it makes a lot of sense, but it would also make you think the Silca tires excel at rolling resistance. Now that Bicycle Rolling Resistance has tested that they are mid-pack, that’s a tough argument to make, too. Silca claims that the RCR is faster than the Vittoria Corsa Pro Control, and BRR confirmed that it’s 3.6 watts faster at 72 psi. That’s a win, but the same testing shows the GP5000 as 1.8 watts faster than the RCR.

I won’t argue that 1.8 watts is worth choosing the GP5000, but is anyone going to argue that the GP5000 is a tire that lacks cornering grip or that the ride feel isn’t good? I might even say the Silca tire has better ride feel, but it’s about as subtle as 1.8 watts. It’s worth noting that Silca also has better puncture protection, but I’m still not convinced any of this is quite enough to get people jumping brands.

The main negative I see here is the lack of a compelling reason for people to switch brands. The Silca RCR 29 is another good tire, but it’s not doing anything special. I, for one, can’t wait for Poertner to crack the aero nut without harming puncture protection or rolling resistance.

This could be the place where the Silca RCR tires gain some converts. The product description has a section that covers “Carbon BeadLock technology,” which is a technology Silca is using to swap the normal Kevlar bead “with non-stretching carbon fiber to eliminate moisture absorption, stretch, and tire wobble for a precise rim fit over the entire lifespan of the tire.”…

title: Supporters of Imran Khan start march on locked-down Islamabad
author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen in Delhi
text:
Pakistani authorities insist marchers calling for former PM to be released from jail will not reach the capital

Imran Khan ’s supporters have begun a march to Islamabad to demand his release from jail after efforts by the government to halt the protest failed.

The march began in the former prime minister’s stronghold province of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa in north-west Pakistan on Sunday, according to leaders of his Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party.

Concerns have grown over the health of the 74-year-old former Pakistan cricket captain who has been in prison since 2023. Party colleagues and family claim he is being held in solitary confinement and has been denied visits by his doctor or relatives despite having a serious eye condition and high blood pressure.

The government had gone to extreme lengths to try to stop PTI holding the long march, including shutting down Islamabad and barricading the capital’s entrances with shipping containers and sandbags. Khan’s three sisters were among those detained last week on grounds of national security.

Two rounds of negotiations between the government and PTI leaders took place over the weekend but broke down when Khan’s allies insisted that he be part of political talks.

Attaullah Tarar, the information minister, accused the PTI of “double standards and hypocrisy”.

Thousands of supporters had joined the protest by Monday afternoon and the crowds are expected to grow on the way to Peshawar, the main city in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which the marchers should reach by Wednesday.

The march is being led by the province’s chief minister, Sohail Afridi, who described those taking part as “Imran Khan’s soldiers”.

“I call upon you all to come out, the youngsters to come out for the sake ​of your leader who is sitting in jail,” he said.

Khan was prime minister from 2018 to 2022, when he was toppled by a parliamentary vote of no confidence. Since then, he and the PTI have faced mounting government pressure, which culminated in his arrest in 2023. The harassment and detention of other PTI leaders continues.

Khan is widely considered the country’s most popular politician, while the ruling coalition government, which is backed by the military, is facing discontent over an economic crisis and a surge in terrorism.

Ministers say the march is illegal and all measures will be taken to ensure it does not break through the capital’s boundaries.

Tens of thousands of police and paramilitary personnel were deployed to Islamabad and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa last week, raising fears that Khan’s supporters will be met with state violence. Government politicians falsely claimed that the PTI was allowing militants from the Pakistan Taliban to take part in the march.

Opposition leaders fear the prime minister will impose emergency rule on Khyber Pakhtunkhwa to stop the march.

title: Six champions crowned, new winners and lap records fall at Castle Combe
‘Speak With Data’: UAE Boss Slams Skeptics Fueling Del Toro-McNulty Conspiracy Theories
author: Jim Cotton
text:
Did Isaac del Toro help his UAE trade teammate Brandon McNulty win the road world title?

That’s the debate that’s doing the rounds after McNulty brought the U.S. its first rainbow jersey in 33 years at the UCI road world championships last weekend.

“Del Toro was obviously working for McNulty,” gnashed Tom Pidcock in the aftermath of a wild race in Montréal.

Michael Matthews insinuated similar as Team USA’s losing rivals picked apart what went wrong last Sunday.

The Tin Foil Hat Brigade has been picking over race replays and sparking conspiracy theories ever since.

Was there a nefarious trade team alliance in this race of nations?

Speaking to QuiBici Sport , McNulty and Del Toro’s manager at UAE Emirates-XRG dismissed the doubters.

If the Mexican Del Toro somehow colluded with Team USA after McNulty slipped away with his decisive attack, Joxean Fernández Matxin wants to see proof.

“To anyone who insinuates this, I urge you to speak with data and not with opinions,” Matxin told Qui Bici Sport . “How long was Del Toro on the front? And the others who are talking, how long were they on the front trying to close it down?

“If you bring me evidence with numbers showing that he pulled less than the others, then I can agree with you,” Matxin said. “But if they are just words, with all due respect, it remains an opinion we can all form.”

Matxin’s words of defense are hardly a surprise.

He’s in the upper tier of management at UAE, the super team boasting Del Toro, McNulty, and Tadej Pogačar on the books and now a third straight year hosting the reigning world champion.

Of course he’ll say McNulty won fair and square.

But even without any possible supporting data, the evidence was all over the TV screens.

Del Toro was the most active rider in the race, despite representing one of cycling’s minnow nations.

“He wanted to win worlds,” Matxin said. “He defends the colors of Mexico because he is proud to be Mexican. He wants to make history for his country.”

Matxin went as far as to say that his Tour de France podium-finisher was the best rider in Montréal.

“In my opinion, Del Toro was the strongest, even if Brandon won. You could see that in how the other riders marked him,” Matxin told QuiBici . “The course may not have been the best for him, but in terms of condition, he was superior to everyone.”

With Pogačar on the sidelines and Remco Evenepoel on an off-day, it was a rainbow opportunity Del Toro would never throw away.

Speaking to Velo last week, Team USA sport director Mike Creed and cult favorite road captain Larry Warbasse also dismissed the collusion conspiracy .

The theory that Del Toro switched passports in the final of road worlds was, according to Warbasse, “ridiculous.”

“You don’t pull all day and then just give the race to McNulty,” Creed told Velo . “If you just finished 270km and you’re frustrated, and your name is Tom Pidcock, that’s understandable.

“For everyone else, it’s just stirring the pot,” Creed continued. “I don’t know anyone who would give away the world championships.”

So why didn’t Del Toro pull the chasers when McNulty launched his winning raid?

One, he was probably gassed. He’d just been riding the front for the best part of 40km.

Two, he was isolated and caught at the opposite end of the spectrum from USA, who flooded the zone with McNulty, Matteo Jorgenson, and Quinn Simmons.

Del Toro wasn’t shy when he debriefed the race to ESPN MX last week.

His rivals exploited Mexico’s collective weakness, and he couldn’t do more when his race started to unravel.

“The peloton raced a little against us or used the fact we didn’t have the best team,” Del Toro told ESPN MX .

“I didn’t want the gold medal to get away from me,” he added. “Finally, though, it was very difficult for me to keep going, and I ran fifth, unfortunately. It’s a bittersweet taste.”

If Team USA paid Del Toro for his role in McNulty’s world title, the Mexican clearly invested in some good acting classes.

Speculation aside, McNulty now owns the rainbow jersey for the next 12 months.

Despite the background debate, the consensus is that the 28-year-old earned the stripes courtesy of individual strength and the smarts of U.S. nationals.

McNulty hasn’t publicly spoken out about the Del Toro drama, and it’s hard to imagine he ever will.

However, the shy Arizonan could barely hide his delight after he debuted his new striped top this weekend in Italy.

McNulty hit 10th at the Giro dell’Emila on Saturday and narrowly missed the win Sunday at Coppa Agostoni.

“For sure it is still settling in, with the jersey and everything,” McNulty said Sunday after he finished second in the six-rider sprint.

“It is super special [being the world champion],” McNulty said Sunday. “I feel like the races pass faster; I don’t really think about kilometers to go anymore. Hopefully that continues. Perhaps it will wear off, and I will go back to suffering, but the last two days have been so special.”

McNulty gets two more shots at winning in rainbows before he shuts down his 2026 season.

The hilly circuits of Tre Valle Varesine await on Wednesday.

Three days later, McNulty teams up at UAE Emirates-XRG with – guess who – Del Toro for a monument brawl with Evenepoel and Paul Seixas at Il Lombardia.

That’s a race where the American and Mexican will race together.

title: F1 needs to have hard look at itself - Sainz
text:
Formula 1 "needs to have a hard look at" itself in the wake of unprecedented software glitches that affected Sunday's Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia, Williams driver Carlos Sainz says.

A bug in the software for a wet-weather engine map led to a number of cars struggling to move on formation laps before the start of the race.

The start had to be abandoned, a new software code issued, and the race eventually got under way an hour and a half later than scheduled.

Sainz, who is a director of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association, said: "It is clear the regulations are extremely complicated for the drivers, for the teams, for the power units and for the manufacturers. Who decided five years ago that this was the direction to go?

"We are doing the best with what we are given as a sport and as regulations. The FIA and F1 are doing the best they can.

"But clearly what was decided four or five years ago was wrong. We need to learn as a sport not to make those mistakes again."

Governing body the FIA has launched a "full review" of the situation.

It arose because there had been very little wet-weather running this year, and the specific circumstances that triggered the bug had not previously arisen.

Red Bull team principal Laurent Mekies said on Monday: "It's a good reminder for all of us that we should probably make sure that complexity doesn't get out of hand and that we keep things as under control as possible.

"And I'm sure we'll have discussions with the teams, with the FIA and with F1 to see how we can protect ourselves from those situations moving forward and make sure we can keep the complexity of the cars and the systems under control."

Sainz's remarks are a reference to the wider debate about this year's new engine regulations, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power.

The engines are fundamentally energy starved, which has led to drivers feeling the cars behave in a counter-intuitive way, and have reduced the impact of driver skill.

The engines have about 1,000bhp on full power, but only 540bhp when the batteries run out.

Because of the way the regulations have been arranged, the batteries are fully deploying and recharging several times a lap. And a series of highly complex restrictions have been introduced relating to the operations of the engine to try to alleviate some of the issues that have arisen.

One of those is what triggered the problem in Malaysia - the total electrical power is reduced from 350kW (470bhp) to 250kW (335bhp) in the wet.

One of the idiosyncrasies of the rules is that the cars slow down at the end of straights to recharge batteries, and many challenging fast corners have been neutered because they are being used as what two-time champion Fernando Alonso has described as "charging stations for the car".

The 50-50 split was decided upon five or six years ago, at a time when road-car manufacturers were pushing electrification.

The rules succeeded in attracting Audi and Ford into F1, and persuading Honda to reverse a plan to quit.

But teams have been warning the FIA since at least 2023 that issues with energy management would arise in the context of the way the rules have been formulated.

The 50-50-split in itself is not the key issue - it's the lack of means to recover sufficient energy to have the engines running at full power for longer.

But the 50-50 split was not addressed in the context of the current energy recovery restrictions until just before the start of this year, when it became apparent how significant the impact of the engines would be.

Since the cars began to run this year, a series of rule changes have been introduced to address the issues.

This year, the total amount of recovery allowed is altered depending on how energy starved a circuit is.

The energy split will become 60-40 in favour of internal combustion in two steps by 2028.

And F1 bosses and engine suppliers are already working on finalising a new engine formula that will introduce power units that are never energy starved.

FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem initially pushed for naturally aspirated V8s with no hybrid at all.

But the current likeliest solution is a V8 turbo with somewhere in the region of 15-25% electrical power, which will mostly be used as a simple push-to-pass system.

title: What’s Brandon McNulty’s Road Worlds Title Worth? Not Much, and a Lot
author: ahood
text:
McNulty celebrates the world title in Montréal and it remains to be seen how much economic windfall it will deliver. (Photo: Filip Bezdek/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

Brandon McNulty ended America’s 33-year drought for a men’s UCI road world title in Montréal, beat a field stacked with cycling’s biggest stars, and earned himself a rainbow jersey.

But the prize money alone won’t make him rich.

That’s the official paycheck for winning one of the sport’s most coveted races. Michael Matthews earned €4,000 for silver, Mathieu van der Poel collected €2,000 for bronze, and everyone else earned no official prize money.

Of course, McNulty was chasing a place in cycling history, not a down payment on a yacht, when he won America’s first elite men’s road title since Lance Armstrong in 1993 .

But what are those stripes really worth?

The prize money is the same for men and women in Montréal, but things get potentially more lucrative once agents, team bonuses, sponsorship deals, and long-term contracts enter the calculation.

First off, professional riders earn their paycheck from their respective trade teams, not from chasing the rainbow bands.

Racing the worlds with national teams is a unique, one-off event each season where money isn’t the primary motivation. It’s for the love of the game.

In fact, racing for the national team rarely earns the riders any extra dosh at all.

USA Cycling does not pay its road riders an appearance fee to compete at the world championships . The U.S. federation — which receives no government funding — covers travel, accommodation, meals, and the support staff behind the race.

The federation also provides coaches, mechanics, soigneurs , and the other staff needed to keep the national squad rolling.

That’s pretty much the same across the entire peloton.

Some riders used to be paid to race worlds when federation budgets were healthier, especially in cycling’s European heartland. Today, most national teams only cover expenses without paying riders simply to take the start.

So even big stars like Van der Poel or newly crowned world champion Demi Vollering do not receive race money from the Dutch federation simply for showing up.

Some riders even had to buy their own plane ticket to Montréal.

New Zealand’s top pro riders had to cover their costs to race in Montréal, and many junior and U23 ranks across many nations had to as well.

Mads Pedersen deserves kudos when he auctioned off some racing memorabilia and contributed funding to help a pair of U23 riders join the Danish squad in Canada.

Magdeleine Vallières paid for her flight to Rwanda and supplementary team fees before winning the women’s road race in Kigali last year.

The payoff was huge after she won Canada’s first elite road world title.

At least she was closer to home in Montréal last month.

Cycling isn’t known for its huge winners’ paychecks anyway , but the worlds is small by any measure.

Despite the world crown being one of cycling’s most prestigious titles, at €8,000, it almost looks like someone forgot to add a zero.

That’s even less than what an individual stage winner receives in the men’s Tour de France at €11,000 , or the winner of the men’s Tour of Flanders at €20,000.

Winning the rainbow jersey might not earn much on race day, but it pays off in many other ways.

Most top pros will have performance bonuses written into their trade-team contracts. One agent told Velo that performance bonuses are packed in for big wins at races like the monuments and the world championships.

The amounts depend on the rider, the team, and what everyone agreed around the negotiating table. Tadej Pogačar, for example, receives €250,000 for winning the stripes from his trade team contract .

The champion wears the rainbow jersey in road races until the next world championships, giving teams such as UAE Emirates-XRG and FDJ United-Suez plenty of publicity and exposure for their sponsors.

Whether McNulty or Vollering received a worlds bonus, and how much, remains private.

A big win like the world title could produce a big “worlds bounce” in terms of salary negotiating power for the right kind of rider.

In McNulty’s case, that’s hard to say because he already settled his long-term future in April when he extended his UAE contract through the end of 2030.

That does not prevent the two sides from renegotiating the deal — like Pogačar recently did with his contract extension through 2032 — but winning in Montréal does not automatically change an existing salary agreement.

When McNulty and UAE signed that deal this spring , it was months before he won the rainbow jersey. Hopefully, a smart agent at least included a winner’s bonus.

One agent told Velo that today’s market places a premium on youth and future potential.

A world crown strengthens McNulty’s palmarès , but it might not bring a huge salary bump, especially with his future already locked in.

Then there is the question of what McNulty might earn beyond his team contract.

Everyone knows pro bike racing is hardly front-page news in the U.S.

In fact, McNulty said he gave only one pre-race interview before his victory, and that was to Belgian broadcaster Sporza .

His victory drew coverage from The New York Times and The Wall Street Journal , both of which cover cycling regularly.

Whether his win translates into wider American exposure remains to be seen, but it’s unlikely he’ll be on a Wheaties box anytime soon.

He might land sponsorship opportunities within cycling and earn appearance fees at critériums and promotional events . There could also be opportunities closer to home in Arizona.

Of course, not everything is about money.

What’s certain is that McNulty will wear the rainbow jersey until the next world championships and the champion’s bands for the rest of his career.

Those stripes put McNulty in rare company, one of just five Americans to win an elite road race world title .

£800m in, £800m out - why Man City scandal shines light on Man Utd finances
text:
The Premier League's statement laid it out in black and white.

'A total of £830.69m, payable and paid by Abu Dhabi United Group (ADUG) to the club'.

In other words, Manchester City 's owners circumvented the league's financial regulations by pumping money into the club.

The damning judgement landed less than five days after Manchester United 's extended filing to the New York Stock Exchange which detailed their end of year accounts to 30 June 2026.

Contained within it was an interest payment of £37m, an increase from £34m the previous year.

And respected football finance blogger Swiss Ramble now estimates that United's net interest payments since the leveraged Glazer takeover of the club in 2005 have risen to a total of £852m.

Without excusing City's owners in any way, it has not escaped the attentions of many fans from both Manchester clubs that while the arrival of one ownership group in the city has resulted in money being ploughed in, with the other, it has meant a similar significant sum being taken out.

United's latest accounts included this comment from chief executive Omar Berrada: "While these results confirm that we are on the right trajectory, we will continue to take a disciplined approach to ensure our finances remain sustainable."

This came after a third-place finish in the Premier League, which confirmed a return to the Champions League after a two-year absence.

Record revenues of £677.6m, projected to go as high as £760m in 2026-27, is something to celebrate.

Yet Berrada's cautious stance underlined a few home truths.

In confirming they had spent £191.7m on new players; notably Carlos Baleba, Andrey Santos and Youri Tielemans, and costs associated with them, plus academy players such as England youth international Tynan Thompson, since 30 June, with payments due 'in the next five years'. United also revealed they had borrowed an additional £90m. It took their overall debt to £1.15bn.

To put that into context, in accounts to June 2021, the comparable sum was £667m.

Prior to 30 June, United's transfer debt was £375m. Of that, £218m must be paid before 30 June 2027. United have also said in addition to Baleba, Santos and Tielemans, they are liable for another £122.8m in potential contract payments if players they have already signed hit pre-agreed targets – although presumably the club would be happy if they ended up paying this.

When they restructured their debt in June, United added $125m (£94.36m) to their main debt. On 23 September, they said £63.5m had been spent on land for their proposed new stadium, the precise funding model for which is still to be determined.

Many fans, particularly those who do not want a new stadium, feel that money would have been better invested in Michael Carrick's squad.

Yet, as Berrada said, United are taking a 'disciplined approach' on that.

In 2025, United had the fifth highest wage bill in the Premier League, at £313m. The absence of European football means that sum dropped to £302m in 2025-26. No other clubs have released their figures yet, but it would be a major surprise if United climbed any higher, meaning Carrick over-achieved by finishing third. United's wages to turnover ratio is 45%. No club had a better figure than that last season.

While there are variables and also notable exceptions, including the Old Trafford outfit themselves who over the past decade, have topped the annual salary cost table but not the actual Premier League, and in 2024-25 finished 15th despite those fifth highest wage costs, there is a general correlation between salaries and performance.

Yet, while United were relatively restrained on the transfer front in terms of spending this summer – their £148m outlay was below that of newly-promoted Ipswich and Hull among others – their recent net spend has been high. The reason for this is clear.

When the most recent transfer window closed on 1 September, they had generated £47m from sales. It put them 11th in the Premier League. Only Liverpool of their 'big six' rivals brought in less.

Since they sold striker Romelu Lukaku to Inter Milan for £74m in 2019, United have only generated more than £25m for a player on four occasions – for Mason Greenwood, Scott McTominay, Rasmus Hojlund and Alejandro Garnacho.

It was instructive this summer a series of young players were sold, either for a lower fee than anticipated in the cases of Radek Vitek and Toby Collyer, who joined Middlesbrough and West Brom respectively, or none, like defenders Tyler Fredricson and James Overy. In all cases though, the transfers included significant sell-on and buy-back clauses, which is part of a strategy by United to generate more revenue from player sales.

In June 2023, Premier League clubs voted to cap future leveraged buyouts at around 65% of a club's value. The move seemed to be in response to ALK Capital's takeover of Burnley in December 2020.

Many United fans feel the move was 18 years too late.

The negativity around Manchester City 's scandal has indirectly, shone a light on the situation at Old Trafford.

Given there is little realistic chance of the substantive debt being paid off, Berrada and his colleagues must navigate the tricky balance of keeping costs under control, trimming the outstanding transfer fees, not extending the revolving credit limit and funding a new stadium – all while spending enough to deliver on the pitch.

In 2017-18, United made £80m in prize money from their run to the Champions League quarter-finals. In 2024-25, they got £31m for reaching the Europa League final. In their recently negotiated shirt deal with Adidas, a £10m annual reduction is applied if the club miss out on reaching the Champions League.

When Carrick sends his team out against bottom-club Tottenham at Old Trafford on 10 October, they will be attempting to drag themselves up from 12th place in the table.…
